extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of formal logic (undergraduate/graduate level); readers learning derivation systems, soundness and completeness
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, evaluation criteria, and constructions for logical derivation systems (sequent calculus, natural deduction, tableaux, axiomatic systems), together with proof-theoretic properties such as soundness, completeness, compactness, and the Deduction Theorem. Also includes constructive lemmas (Lindenbaum) and the canonical model construction from complete consistent sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete derivation system is strong enough to show that α is a theorem whenever α is valid, and that Γ ⊢ α whenever Γ ⊨ α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness is harder to establish; some logics have no complete derivation systems. First-order logic does — Gödel proved completeness for a first-order derivation system. The ‘only if’ direction of the equivalence between consistency and satisfiability amounts to completeness (consistency guarantees satisfiability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivation system is sound if it cannot derive things that do not actually hold: every derivable α is valid; if Γ ⊢ α then Γ ⊨ α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soundness is a safety property for derivation systems. Theorem 37B proves soundness by induction on the length of derivations: axioms are tautologies and modus ponens preserves semantic consequence. Consequences: if ⊢ α then α is a tautology, and satisfiable Γ are consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency (syntactic) vs. Satisfiability (semantic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of sentences is called inconsistent if anything whatsoever can be derived from it, and consistent otherwise; inconsistency is the syntactic counterpart to unsatisfiability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We want consistency to coincide with satisfiability: Γ is consistent iff Γ is satisfiable. The ‘only if’ direction is completeness; the ‘if’ direction is soundness. System-specific definitions: in axiomatic systems Γ inconsistent iff Γ ⊢ ⊥; in sequent calculus iff there is derivation of Γ0 ⇒ (empty right side); in tableaux iff there is a closed tableau for the T-assumptions from Γ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequent Calculus: correctness criteria for sequents and derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequents are expressions α1,...,αm ⇒ β1,...,βn; derivations are trees of sequents with initial sequents (axioms) at the leaves and rules of inference manipulating left/right sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules either manipulate the sequences (add/remove/rearrange) or introduce complex wff in the conclusion (examples: ∧L allows inference from α,Γ ⇒ Δ to α∧β,Γ ⇒ Δ; →R allows from α,Γ ⇒ Δ,β to Γ ⇒ Δ, α→β). Γ ⊢ α iff some Γ0 ⊆ Γ yields a derivation with root sequent Γ0 ⇒ α. Sequent-calculus inconsistency: derivation of Γ0 ⇒ (empty right). Sequent calculus is systematic and symmetric, often easy to find derivations but sometimes hard to read and connect to traditional proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Deduction: use and management of assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural deduction formalizes common proof patterns via introduction and elimination rules for each connective; it uses assumptions which may be discharged by certain rules (e.g., →Intro discharges an assumption α when deriving α→β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivations are trees of wffs with leaves as assumptions; discharged assumptions are tracked via labels. Γ ⊢ α holds iff there is a derivation ending in α whose undischarged leaves are in Γ. Natural deduction mirrors mathematicians' reasoning (proof by cases, indirect proof, conditional proof) and is favored for readability and proof-theoretic semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tableaux: signed-formula procedure and closure criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tableaux operate with signed formulas T α and F α in a downward-branching tree; rules add signed subformulas or split branches. A tableau is closed if every branch contains both T α and F α for some α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Γ ⊢ α iff there is some finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ such that there is a closed tableau for {F α, T β1,...,T βn}. Tableaux are very systematic and lend themselves to implementation; if a tableau is open and saturated, a satisfying structure can be read off an open branch. Closed tableaux correspond (up to orientation) to condensed sequent-calculus derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic Derivations: criteria for valid derivation steps
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivation is a finite sequence of sentences where each sentence is either an axiom, an element of Γ, or follows by a rule of inference (e.g., modus ponens) from earlier lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axioms are instances of fixed schemas (examples provided for propositional connectives, eq. (3.1)–(3.14)). Modus ponens (MP) is the prototypical rule: if β and β→α occur earlier, then α is justified. α is a theorem if derivable from the empty set. Axiomatic systems are simple in structure but often cumbersome for constructing proofs in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of Inference (general criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule of inference gives a sufficient condition for when a step in a derivation is correct (an if-then statement referencing prior lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the trivial rule 'if α ∈ Γ then α is a correct inference step' and modus ponens. The set of allowed rules determines what counts as a correct derivation and thus what the ⊢ relation captures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivability relation (⊢) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ ⊢ α iff there is a derivation from Γ whose last sentence is α; α is a theorem if ⊢ α (derivable from empty set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central syntactic relation; different systems (sequent, natural deduction, axiomatic, tableaux) give operational definitions of what constitutes a derivation, but all yield a ⊢ relation used to state soundness/completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency notions in different calculi
rubrics_metrics.description: How inconsistency is recognized depends on the system: in natural deduction Γ inconsistent iff Γ ⊢ ⊥; in sequent calculus if there is derivation of Γ0 ⇒ (empty right side); in tableaux if there is a closed tableau for T-assumptions from Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From an inconsistent set, rules like ⊥I or WR allow deriving any sentence (Explosion/Ex Falso Quodlibet). Recognizing inconsistency is important for completeness and compactness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: System design trade-offs (readability, ease of proof search, implementability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive evaluation of proof systems: sequent calculus and tableaux are systematic and good for proof search/implementation, but derivations/tableaux can be hard to read and their connection to natural proofs may be obscure; axiomatic systems are simple in structure but hard to use for finding proofs; natural deduction mirrors human reasoning and is easier to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a system, weigh systematicity and symmetry (good for metatheory and automation) against readability and correspondence to handwritten proofs. Tableaux particularly lend themselves to computer implementation; sequent calculi are elegant for derivation theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexivity, Monotonicity, Transitivity (structural properties of ⊢)
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic meta-properties: if α ∈ Γ then Γ ⊢ α (Reflexivity); if Γ ⊆ Δ and Γ ⊢ α then Δ ⊢ α (Monotonicity); if Γ ⊢ α and {α} ∪ Δ ⊢ β then Γ ∪ Δ ⊢ β (Transitivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties are proved straightforwardly from the definition of derivation and are used repeatedly in later metatheory (e.g., compactness, deduction theorem, completeness proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ ⊢ α then there is a finite subset Γ0 ⊆ Γ such that Γ0 ⊢ α. Equivalently, if every finite subset of Γ is consistent, then Γ is consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compactness follows from the finiteness of derivations; it also follows from completeness and can be proved directly via the same sort of constructions used in the completeness proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ ∪ {α} ⊢ β if and only if Γ ⊢ α → β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is proved by induction on derivation length; it relies on chosen axioms (eq. (3.7), (3.8)) so that conditionalization works. The Deduction Theorem is a key meta-result used to move between assumptions and implications in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Useful syntactic consequences and rules (Explosion, Double Negation, Contraposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proved syntactic facts used in proofs: {α, ¬α} ⊢ β (Ex Falso Quodlibet); {¬¬α} ⊢ α (Double Negation Elimination); contraposition style results: if Γ ∪ {¬α} ⊢ ¬β then Γ ∪ {β} ⊢ α, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These follow from the axioms and MP and are used in derivations about consistency and completeness (e.g., Proposition 34C items). They serve as canonical proof patterns to manipulate negation and implication syntactically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete set (definition and properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set Γ is complete iff for any sentence α, either α ∈ Γ or ¬α ∈ Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete consistent sets are central to the completeness proof: from a complete consistent Γ* one can define a valuation (set truth assignment) making exactly the propositional variables in Γ* true and then prove by induction that v ⊨ α iff α ∈ Γ*. Proposition 42B lists closure properties (e.g., α→β ∈ Γ iff α ∉ Γ or β ∈ Γ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lindenbaum's Lemma (extend to complete consistent set)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any consistent set Γ can be extended to some set Γ* that is both consistent and complete by adding sentences one at a time while preserving consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The constructive proof enumerates all sentences and at each step adds either α or ¬α provided consistency is maintained. The union of all stages is a complete consistent superset used to build the canonical model for the completeness theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical model construction from a complete consistent set
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a complete consistent set Γ*, define a valuation v so that v(p) = T iff p ∈ Γ* (for atomic p); then prove v ⊨ α iff α ∈ Γ*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This valuation is used to show any consistent Γ is satisfiable by extending Γ to Γ* and using Lemma 44B (induction on formula structure). This is the heart of the completeness/model-existence argument.
